faq.question: How to get my diplomas recognized?
faq.answer: Contact the qualifications recognition body of the target country (e.g. ENIC-NARIC in Europe). The procedure usually takes 2-3 months.

faq.question: Do I need a work permit?
faq.answer: It depends on your nationality and destination country. EU/EEA citizens generally don't need a permit to work in the EU.

recherche.title: Search steps
steps: Choose the neighborhood according to your priorities (work, schools, transport)

tips: Plan 2-3 months of rent for the security deposit
Use local classified ads websites
Beware of scams: never pay before viewing
Check the property condition and do a detailed inventory

faq.question: What budget to plan for housing?
faq.answer: Plan 30-40% of your income for rent. Add 2-3 months of rent for initial deposit and agency fees.

faq.question: How to rent without local history?
faq.answer: Offer a guarantor, pay several months in advance, or use services like Garantme to reassure landlords.

france.alertText: Social Security covers 70% of medical costs. A supplementary health plan (~€70/month) covers the remaining costs. Long-term conditions (ALD) are fully covered at 100%.

usa.alertText: No universal coverage. Health insurance is usually tied to employer. Marketplace (ACA): ~$450/month on average. Uninsured care is extremely expensive. Visit healthcare.gov.

japan.alertTitle: National Health Insurance (国民健康保険)
japan.alertText: Health insurance is mandatory in Japan. Residents pay ~30% of care (70% reimbursed). NHI costs about ¥25,000/month. Dental and optical care partially covered.

switzerland.alertText: Basic health insurance (LAMal) is MANDATORY for all residents. Among the highest premiums in Europe (~393 CHF/month). Dental and optical care NOT covered by LAMal.

jp.partTime: Part-time (パート / アルバイト)

france.0: EU citizens: no work permit required
france.2: Talent Passport: qualified profiles (master's degree + salary ≥ €53,836/yr)
france.3: Long-stay work visa: contract + validated authorization
france.4: WHV (Working Holiday Visa): 18-30 years, partner countries, 1-2 years

uk.0: EU citizens post-Brexit: Skilled Worker visa required
uk.1: Skilled Worker visa: minimum salary £38,700/yr (£29,000 for some roles)
uk.2: Health and Care Worker visa: NHS and care sector
uk.3: Graduate visa: 2 years for UK graduates
uk.4: Youth Mobility Scheme: 18-30 years, partner countries, 2 years

ch.4: Documents: Contract, Passport, Criminal record, Full CV

us.3: Green Card: permanent residence (employer or family sponsorship)
us.4: OPT/CPT: internships for international students (F-1 visa)

ca.0: Express Entry program: skilled immigration (CRS points)
ca.1: LMIA: employer authorization + closed work permit

de.0: EU citizens: free movement, no permit needed
de.1: EU Blue Card: recognized degree + salary ≥ €45,300/yr (or €41,042 for shortage occupations)
de.2: Job seeker residence permit: 6 months to search (recognized degree required)
de.4: Aufenthaltserlaubnis: residence permit tied to employer

au.0: Skilled Worker visa (subclass 482): employer sponsorship, 2-4 years
au.1: Skilled Independent visa (subclass 189): points-based, permanent residence
au.4: Skills Assessment mandatory by sector-specific body

jp.0: Categorical work visa: engineer, humanities, business management
jp.1: Highly Skilled Professional visa: points system (70+ points)
jp.2: Specified Skilled Worker (特定技能): 14 shortage sectors
jp.3: Working Holiday: 18-30 years, partner countries, 1 year
jp.4: Employer sponsorship MANDATORY for all work visas

france.0: French essential (B2 minimum) except some tech startups
france.1: CV + cover letter mandatory, professional photo recommended
france.2: Trial period: 2-4 months negotiable, free termination without compensation
france.3: Unemployment: 57% of salary for 18-24 months if sufficient contributions
france.4: 35h legal workweek with possibility of overtime bonuses (+25% then +50%)

uk.1: Anglo-Saxon CV: max 2 pages, no photo, no date of birth
uk.2: Right to Work check mandatory: passport + visa/BRP/settled status
uk.3: Notice period: 1 week to 3 months depending on contract and seniority
uk.4: Universal Credit: unemployment/housing aid based on income and situation

ch.0: Language by region: German (Zurich, Bern), French (Geneva, Lausanne), Italian (Ticino)
ch.1: Very high salaries BUT very high cost of living (rent, health, transport)
ch.2: Swiss CV: photo mandatory, detailed degrees, verified references
ch.3: Work permit required BEFORE applying (except EU/EFTA)
ch.4: Trial period: 1-3 months, termination possible with short notice

us.0: Professional English essential (no federal official language)
us.1: Resume (not CV): 1 page max, no photo, results-oriented with numbers
us.2: At-will employment: termination possible without cause in most states
us.3: Health coverage often tied to employer (no universal system)
us.4: Intense networking culture: LinkedIn, meetups, industry events

ca.0: Officially bilingual: English everywhere, French in Quebec (OQLF requires French at work)
ca.1: Canadian CV: 2 pages max, no photo, no age, achievement-oriented
ca.2: Highly structured immigration: Express Entry + PNP = main pathways
ca.3: Employment Insurance (EI): federal unemployment if sufficient contributions

de.0: German essential for most positions (B2-C1), English accepted in tech/startups
de.1: German CV (Lebenslauf): professional photo, reverse chronological, very detailed
de.2: Strong diploma culture: Anabin / KMK recognition often required
de.3: High social contributions (~40% of gross) but comprehensive coverage

au.1: Australian CV: 2-3 pages, no photo, with referees (2 references min)
au.2: Relaxed but professional culture, flexible hours common
au.3: Superannuation (retirement): employer pays 11.5% on top of salary
au.4: Fair Work Act: worker rights strongly protected, high minimum wage

jp.0: Japanese often required (JLPT N2-N1), English accepted in tech/international finance
jp.1: Rirekisho (履歴書): standard Japanese CV format, photo mandatory, sometimes handwritten
jp.2: Intense work culture: frequent overtime, teamwork paramount
jp.3: Seniority system (年功序列): progression tied to tenure, evolving
jp.4: Shūkatsu (就活): standardized recruitment season for new graduates
